summary: The tutorial explains a hand-animated product-camera style built from short momentum motifs rather than a single smooth point-to-point move. A major move is split into anticipation, main travel and recovery; static sections receive a subtle vertical middle key; depth-of-field values are synchronized with camera keys; and a Track To target Empty is animated independently to control attention and add operator-like reaction lag.

observed_project_context.delivery_orientation: vertical 2160 × 3840 visible in Blender output settings
observed_project_context.visible_workspace: camera/render preview on the left, 3D scene viewport on the right, Dope Sheet at the bottom

techniques.name: Four-key momentum motif
steps: K1 establishes the current pose.
K2 moves slightly opposite the intended direction to gather momentum.
K3 performs the main fast move.
K4 rebounds or settles slightly back from the extreme.
techniques.production_note: Treat this as a local motion motif, not a fixed universal timing rule. Gate acceleration and overshoot in the Graph Editor.

techniques.name: Floating hold
steps: Find two hold keys with identical or near-identical transforms.
Insert a middle Location key.
Offset it slightly on Z, then return to the original pose.
techniques.production_note: Optional stylistic motion. Disable it when a true still frame is needed for identity, compositing or AI video conditioning.

techniques.name: Focus keys synchronized with camera keys
steps: At every important camera pose, inspect subject sharpness.
Adjust focus distance with fine increments.
Insert a focus-distance key and, when required, an f-stop key at the same frame.
techniques.production_note: Manual focus pulls are deliberate but tedious. A focus object can be evaluated as a more robust alternative when exact target tracking is desired.

techniques.name: Independent animated Track To target
steps: Create an Empty near the subject with Shift+A.
Add a Track To constraint to the camera and set the Empty as target.
Animate the Empty toward successive visual attention points.
Offset target keys a few frames behind fast subject motion for operator-like reaction.
techniques.production_note: The transcript phrase about reaction time is noisy; visual evidence supports a delay of a few frames, not seconds.

techniques.name: Frame-rate aware timing
steps: Author demonstrates at 60 fps.
Convert frame offsets proportionally for 24 or 30 fps instead of copying numbers literally.

workflow_recipe.name: DRUMBOII four-key hero camera
steps: Audit the target asset and establish a clean camera composition.
Create ROOT, camera and TARGET Empty controls.
Add Track To from camera to TARGET.
Build K1–K4 for the camera using anticipation, main move and recovery.
Add a middle Z key only where a floating hold is stylistically appropriate.
Animate TARGET between visual interest points, optionally lagging subject motion by a few frames.
Key focus distance/f-stop with major camera poses or validate an explicit focus object.
Inspect F-Curves for speed continuity and overshoot.
Render a marker-based gate before saving.
gates: K2 anticipation is perceptible but not distracting
K3 main move preserves subject identity and avoids clipping
K4 recovery does not oscillate indefinitely
focus remains intentional at every hero pose
target lag feels human rather than erroneous

asset_specific_applications.recommended_move: short dolly reveal with restrained recovery
three-quarter push with target shift from screen to controls
vertical crane or focus pull across the open clamshell
target-led tilt with delayed attention shift
low three-quarter tracking move; optimize before large duplication
simple scale-reference or fast anticipation insert

risks: The tutorial demonstrates many hand-authored keys but does not explain exact interpolation/handle settings.
The 60 fps frame values cannot be copied directly into the current 24 fps Pulsed workflow.
Micro-floating holds conflict with shots that require a genuinely static conditioning frame.
Manual focus-distance keying can drift if the subject or target changes after animation.
Too much anticipation or recovery produces a toy-like wobble instead of believable camera mass.
open_questions: Which interpolation and handle types were used in the source project?
Were camera rotations directly keyed or fully produced by the Track To target?
What exact frame delay was used for the reaction-lag example?
Is f-stop animated for exposure/look, depth-of-field shape, or both?
